title: Chest Pain Again After a Heart Attack at 46 / Avoid Routine Angiography

blocks.text: Chest Pain Again After a Heart Attack at 46 / Avoid Routine Angiography

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-37 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and Acute Cardiovascular Care Association position paper on spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Adlam D et al, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3353-3368); American Heart Association scientific statement on spontaneous coronary artery dissection (Hayes SN et al, Circulation 2018;137:e523-e557) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 46-year-old school receptionist. Spontaneous coronary artery dissection was diagnosed at angiography three weeks ago after a heart attack, and she was treated with tablets alone. She has had two further episodes of chest tightness this week. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A heart attack from a coronary artery tear in a woman in her forties is a different disease from ordinary coronary disease. The station turns on careful assessment of new chest pain, avoiding unnecessary angiography, and the long-term plan.

The Examiner Trap. She is anxious and wants another angiogram, or her pain is dismissed as anxiety. Candidates either rush her back for angiography or reassure with no ECG. Pass: ECG and troponin, conservative approach, plan. Fail: no tests or routine repeat angiography.

Ask about the pain, its pattern and triggers, then her tablets, her pregnancy plans, her mood and her exercise.
"Describe the tightness. What brings it on? Are you taking your tablets? Do you plan more children? How is your mood?"
Pain; triggers; duration; breathlessness; drugs; contraception; pregnancy plans; mood; exercise; migraine.
Check the blood pressure, pulse and heart, look for signs of heart failure and for fibromuscular dysplasia clues.
"May I check your blood pressure in both arms, your pulse, heart, chest and neck? Tell me if anything hurts."
Blood pressure both arms; pulse; heart sounds; chest; neck bruits; ankles; cover her.
Explain the diagnosis and the plan: tests for the new pain, long-term tablets, a scan of other arteries and rehabilitation.
"Your artery tore rather than blocked, so treatment is different. I'd like an ECG and blood test today."
ECG; troponin; admission; aspirin; beta-blocker; blood pressure; scan; rehabilitation; pregnancy; mood.

Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): discharges her with recurrent chest pain and no ECG or troponin.

Admits if the ECG or troponin is abnormal; keeps low-dose aspirin, considers a beta-blocker, controls blood pressure, arranges cardiac rehabilitation, and tells her to call 999 if the pain returns severe or does not settle.
Also advises avoiding high-intensity or contact sport, and counselling before any pregnancy by a team, including a review of tablets that are unsafe in pregnancy such as ramipril.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 46-year-old school receptionist. You are tearful, exhausted and frightened of another attack.
Opening line: "I've had the tight chest again twice this week. I'm terrified it's another one. Do I need another angiogram?"
Volunteered: you are on aspirin, a beta-blocker and a tablet for blood pressure (ramipril). No allergies. You have never smoked and drink little alcohol.
Only if asked: each episode lasted about ten minutes and came on when you were stressed, not exercising. No breathlessness. You get migraines.
Only if asked about children: you have two children, and you would like another baby; your husband agrees. Contraception: condoms only; you stopped the pill when you were admitted. No recent travel.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you will die in front of your children. Say: "I can't stop checking my pulse."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it happening again?" "Will I have another one?" "Can I have another baby?"
How you react: if brushed off, you leave frightened. If listened to and told the tests, you engage. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: anxious, comfortable at rest; respiratory rate 16; pulse 64 regular; blood pressure 126/76 right arm and 124/76 left arm; temperature 36.6 °C. Heart sounds normal. Chest clear. No oedema. No neck bruits.
Results, only when requested: ECG: normal. High-sensitivity troponin: not raised. CT of the head to the pelvis, if requested: changes of fibromuscular dysplasia in the renal arteries.
Question ladder: 1. Why was she managed conservatively? (E) 2. Why is repeat angiography avoided? (E) 3. Which tests for the new pain? (E) 4. Which tablets? (E) 5. What about another pregnancy? (E)

Curveballs: She asks for angiography to be sure: only with hard evidence of ischaemia. She asks about running a marathon: avoid high-intensity and competitive contact sport. She develops ongoing pain with ST changes: emergency pathway.

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): recurrent pain after a heart attack needs an ECG and troponin. No consent, no examination, and routine angiography requested with no reasoning.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I check your blood pressure in both arms, your pulse, heart and chest? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]

CANDIDATE: What brings the tightness on? Any breathlessness? Are you taking your tablets? What contraception do you use, and do you plan more children? How is your mood, and how much are you exercising? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Stress. I take them all. I'd like another baby.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, then covers her.) Equal blood pressures, a regular pulse, normal heart sounds, a clear chest and no oedema. Thank you for letting me examine you. [R3 Pass] [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I need an ECG and troponin today to exclude new ischaemia. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Angiography is reserved for clear evidence of ischaemia, because the artery is fragile and a catheter can tear it. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: If either test is abnormal, I'd admit you. You'll stay on aspirin, with blood pressure control and cardiac rehabilitation. If the tightness comes back severe or does not settle, call 999 and don't drive yourself. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: Dying in front of my kids.
CANDIDATE: That is a fair fear; most tears heal. [R7 Pass] Shall we do the tests now? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Tested for new ischaemia and avoided routine angiography. Did not name vasospasm, the scan for other arteries, pregnancy counselling or sport.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? It's hard to be frightened of your own heart. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Do you get migraines or headaches? Is your blood pressure well controlled? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) No neck bruits, and equal arm pressures. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Vasospasm, a new dissection and a non-cardiac cause are possible. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: I'd also scan your other arteries from head to pelvis for fibromuscular dysplasia. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Avoid high-intensity and contact sport, and see a team before any pregnancy. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll screen for anxiety, depression and post-traumatic stress. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, migraine, other causes, the arterial scan, sport and pregnancy advice, mood screening and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about pregnancy plans. It changes the long-term plan.
R4: Calling it anxiety. New pain after a heart attack needs an ECG and troponin.
R5: Requesting routine repeat angiography. The friable artery can be torn by the catheter.
R6: Discharging with no tests. New ischaemia must be excluded.
"Can I ask whether you plan any more children?"
"New pain after a heart attack needs an ECG and a blood test today."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

ESC position paper 2018 (Adlam et al): spontaneous coronary artery dissection causes about a quarter of heart attacks in women under 50 (24% in a Canadian series; up to 35% in others, AHA 2018). Angiography is the principal diagnostic test; intracoronary imaging can be considered when the diagnosis is uncertain, but any catheter work carries a risk of iatrogenic dissection. Where flow is maintained and there is no ongoing ischaemia, a conservative approach is preferred; most lesions heal over a few months. For recurrent chest pain, use serial ECG and high-sensitivity troponin and reserve invasive angiography for hard evidence of ischaemia or myocardial necrosis.

Treatment is based on observational data (ESC 2018): most authors advocate aspirin, often with clopidogrel in the acute phase, for an uncertain duration; in one cohort beta-blockers were associated with fewer recurrences and hypertension with more, but this is unproven. Assess left ventricular function. AHA 2018: refer to cardiac rehabilitation; avoid prolonged high-intensity activity, highly competitive or contact sports and Valsalva during lifting; consider vascular imaging from the brain to the pelvis for fibromuscular dysplasia in all patients.

ESC 2018: it is reasonable to avoid hormonal contraception where possible; any pregnancy should be treated as high risk, with careful counselling beforehand, a multidisciplinary team and potentially teratogenic drugs stopped. AHA 2018: many clinicians advise against pregnancy, though data are few, and tertiary preconception counselling is advised; depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress are common after SCAD.
THINK: SCAD, new pain: ECG and troponin, not routine angiography.
SAY: "Your artery tore rather than blocked, so treatment differs."
DO: Both-arm blood pressure; ask pregnancy plans.
NUMBERS: Conservative if stable and no ongoing ischaemia (ESC 2018); brain-to-pelvis imaging for FMD (AHA 2018).
TRAP: Anxiety label; routine angiogram.
FINISH: ECG, troponin, aspirin, blood pressure, rehab, team.
